title: Diarrhoea on immunotherapy for melanoma — recognise, investigate and act safely

blocks.text: Diarrhoea on immunotherapy for melanoma — recognise, investigate and act safely

AMaC MRCP PACES23 | Round 5 | R5-236 | Station 2: acute consultation | 20 minutes | Communication, clinical judgement and patient welfare (C, E, F, G) | AMaC educational scoring, not official PACES marks

A 56-year-old receiving pembrolizumab for melanoma reports six loose stools daily, abdominal cramps and reduced oral intake. Take a focused history, determine urgency and explain your plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: Hook: Suspected immune checkpoint inhibitor colitis, but infectious diarrhoea including C. difficile must be considered. Grade severity by stool frequency above baseline and systemic findings. Trap: Grade-specific treatment and decisions on rechallenge require oncology leadership; do not imply every mild case requires systemic steroids.

rows: “First, I want to check how unwell you are.”
Assess stability and the specific emergency signs.
“I’ll ask questions that help us distinguish the causes.”
Ask baseline stool frequency, daily increase, blood or mucus, pain, fever, dehydration, recent antibiotics, travel and other immune-related symptoms; assess observations and abdominal tenderness.
“I will arrange tests and support appropriate to the risk.”

Contact oncology the same day; withhold further checkpoint inhibitor treatment pending specialist review for significant suspected colitis; obtain bloods, stool infection screen and assess dehydration. Oncology guides systemic corticosteroids and escalation if severe or refractory.
“I will explain when we must act urgently.”
Severe pain, peritonism, haemodynamic instability, fever, bloody stools or marked dehydration requires emergency hospital assessment; avoid simply prescribing antidiarrhoeals and sending home.

Asks baseline stools and grades by daily increase, plus pain, blood, fever or dehydration
Recognises systemic compromise can indicate severe colitis regardless of frequency
Asks onset, baseline, stool number, blood, abdominal pain and recent antibiotics
Reviews infection exposures and other immune toxicities
Automatically gives steroids without checking infection
Considers checkpoint-inhibitor colitis and infection, including C difficile
Checks for acute abdomen, perforation or toxic megacolon
Offers no assessment until next cycle
Urgently checks observations, hydration, FBC, renal function, CRP and stool infection studies
Liaises with acute oncology/gastroenterology for imaging and endoscopy when indicated
Advises continuing pembrolizumab with moderate/severe symptoms
Withholds immunotherapy and obtains urgent oncology advice for suspected grade 2+ colitis
Uses specialist-directed corticosteroids after appropriate assessment and escalates if severe or refractory
Escalates severe pain, bloody diarrhoea, fever or dehydration to emergency evaluation
Documents grading and creates follow-up and steroid monitoring plan

blocks.text: Patient is concerned about the symptoms and asks: ““Should I carry on my cancer treatment?”” The role-player provides symptoms from the brief and relevant positive/negative history only when asked; avoid volunteering the diagnosis. Respond to clear empathetic explanations.

THINK: Suspected immune checkpoint inhibitor colitis, but infectious diarrhoea including C. difficile must be considered. Grade severity by stool frequency above baseline and systemic findings. SAY: avoid certainty without confirmation. DO: Contact oncology the same day; withhold further checkpoint inhibitor treatment pending specialist review for significant suspected colitis; obtain bloods, stool infection screen and assess dehydration. Oncology guides systemic corticosteroids and escalation if severe or refractory. NUMBERS: 20-minute encounter. TRAP: Grade-specific treatment and decisions on rechallenge require oncology leadership; do not imply every mild case requires systemic steroids. FINISH: Severe pain, peritonism, haemodynamic instability, fever, bloody stools or marked dehydration requires emergency hospital assessment; avoid simply prescribing antidiarrhoeals and sending home.
